title: Syno: Structured Synthesis for Neural Operators
problem: Neural architecture search (NAS) and tensor compilers both optimize over existing manually designed operators and cannot discover fundamentally new operator designs with better accuracy-performance tradeoffs. There is no systematic method to automatically synthesize novel neural operators that satisfy structural constraints required for trainability and hardware efficiency.
method: Syno defines a set of fine-grained primitives operating on tensor dimensions that enforce properties needed for stable model training (e.g., dimension matching, associativity). Expression canonicalization techniques prune redundant candidates during search. A guided synthesis flow constrains valid operators to specified input/output dimension sizes, and stochastic tree search (Monte Carlo-style) efficiently explores the large design space. The resulting operators are compiled and evaluated on real hardware.

title: Evaluating Ruche Networks: Physically Scalable, Cost-Effective, Bandwidth-Flexible NoCs
problem: The standard 2-D mesh NoC topology suffers poor latency and throughput scaling for data-intensive manycore workloads, while prior solutions (concentrated routers, widened channels) rely on outdated assumptions that break under modern streaming-bandwidth requirements and impose significant additional cost. A rigorous, RTL-level evaluation of Ruche Networks as a superior alternative has not been performed.
method: Ruche Networks augment the 2-D mesh topology with uniform long-range bypass links (Ruche channels) that allow non-neighboring routers to communicate in fewer hops, preserving the physical scalability and regular structure of the mesh. The authors implement Ruche Networks at RTL level and compare against 2-D mesh and torus topologies under identical conditions, evaluating network throughput, latency, power consumption, area efficiency, and cycle time across manycore workloads with streaming bandwidth demands.

title: ArtMem: Adaptive Migration in Reinforcement Learning-Enabled Tiered Memory
problem: Tiered memory systems struggle with three key inefficiencies: existing migration policies perform inconsistently across workloads, fail to adapt when the fast-tier access rate is low, and miss opportunities to tune migration scope dynamically based on workload patterns, causing unnecessary page migrations.
method: ArtMem is a reinforcement learning (RL)-driven tiered memory management framework that dynamically adapts migration policy to evolving workload behavior. The RL agent observes fast-tier access rates and workload access patterns at runtime to decide page placement, migration scope (which pages to migrate and how many), and when to suppress migration entirely when the fast tier is underutilized. This closed-loop control replaces static thresholds with learned policies.

title: Will We Ever have Truly Secure Operating Systems?
problem: Operating system kernels remain a dominant attack surface despite decades of security research; formal proofs of OS security have historically been limited to small microkernels and have not scaled to binary-level or general-purpose OS kernels.
method: The paper surveys the seL4 microkernel verification program, which produced a proof chain from C implementation correctness, down to binary-level verification, through to security enforcement proofs (confidentiality, integrity) and sound worst-case execution-time analysis, covering 4 ISAs. The approach uses interactive theorem provers (Isabelle/HOL) to formally connect abstract security policies to compiled binary behavior, then discusses speculative early-stage work on extending this methodology to a provably secure general-purpose OS.

title: Selectively Uniform Concurrency Testing
problem: Randomized concurrency testing algorithms fail to uniformly sample thread interleavings, causing them to miss bugs that manifest only in rare, infrequent interleavings. Prior algorithms are biased in their sampling, leading to poor coverage of the exponentially large interleaving space.
method: SURW (Selectively Uniform Random Walk) is an online randomized concurrency testing algorithm that achieves interleaving-uniformity by carefully selecting a subset of program events and applying a uniform sampling strategy over their interleaving space. The algorithm operates as a black-box randomized technique that requires only minimal additional information about the program to achieve uniformity over broad classes of programs and arbitrary event subsets.

title: Wave: Offloading Resource Management to SmartNIC Cores
problem: Userspace system software tasks (kernel thread scheduling, memory management, RPC stacks) consume scarce host CPU cores in cloud servers, reducing the compute available to paying tenants. Existing SmartNIC offload frameworks require custom APIs and cannot handle microsecond-scale system software latencies without host CPU involvement.
method: Wave is a framework that runs existing Linux userspace system software (unchanged or minimally modified) as processes/agents on mid-tier SmartNIC ARM cores. It introduces a new host-SmartNIC communication API designed to support microsecond-scale decision latencies, enabling offload of preemption-sensitive tasks such as the kernel thread scheduler. The framework uses Linux userspace system interfaces to align host OS functionality with SmartNIC capabilities, and avoids requiring custom kernel modifications on the host side.

title: Folded Banks: 3D-Stacked HBM Design for Fine-Grained Random-Access Bandwidth
problem: HBM has seen substantial improvements in sequential (peak) bandwidth across generations but irregular/random-access bandwidth has stagnated, limiting performance for applications with non-sequential memory access patterns such as graph analytics, recommendation, and sparse workloads.
method: Folded Banks (FB-HBM) redistributes DRAM bank subarrays by folding them across multiple dies in a 3D stack and relocating command/control logic and global sense amplifiers to a new dedicated base layer implemented in a logic process. Intra-bank column select lines (CSLs) and master data lines (MDLs) are routed vertically through thin-pitch through-silicon vias (TSVs) and hybrid bonds, dramatically reducing RC power losses from long horizontal routing. Self-timed sense amplifiers eliminate the need for costly dummy subarrays, further reducing power and area on the DRAM dies.

title: Spindle: Efficient Distributed Training of Multi-Task Large Models via Wavefront Scheduling
problem: Training multi-task, multi-modal (MT MM) foundation models is inefficient because their heterogeneous model components and diverse workloads across tasks and modalities create complex dependency patterns that existing parallelism strategies cannot jointly optimize. No existing distributed training system addresses the combined challenges of workload heterogeneity and dependency-driven execution scheduling for MT MM models.
method: Spindle decomposes MT MM model execution into 'waves'—groups of heterogeneous micro-tasks—and applies a two-phase joint optimization: (1) heterogeneity-aware workload parallelization that assigns tasks to devices accounting for differing compute demands per modality, and (2) dependency-driven wavefront scheduling that pipelines waves based on their inter-task data dependencies. The wavefront schedule coordinates execution so that waves from different tasks and modalities overlap in time, filling pipeline bubbles caused by load imbalance.

title: GraphPipe: Improving Performance and Scalability of DNN Training with Graph Pipeline Parallelism
problem: Existing pipeline-parallel DNN training systems partition models into sequential stages, ignoring the actual DAG topology of modern neural networks, which causes missed model-parallelism opportunities and suboptimal device utilization.
method: GraphPipe introduces graph pipeline parallelism, which partitions a DNN's computation graph (DAG) rather than a linear sequence into pipeline stages. The system represents the DNN as a dataflow graph, identifies parallelizable subgraphs, and maps them to device groups that execute concurrently in a pipeline fashion. A graph-aware scheduling algorithm determines micro-batch execution order across non-linear pipeline stages to maximize throughput and minimize pipeline bubbles, coordinating across branches of the DAG.

title: CaMDN: Enhancing Cache Efficiency for Multi-tenant DNNs on Integrated NPUs
problem: Multi-tenant DNN execution on shared SoC NPUs suffers from cache contention that degrades performance; shared cache impact on multi-tenant scenarios not well studied.
method: Architecture-scheduling co-design: lightweight hardware support for model-exclusive cache regions controlled by NPU; cache-aware mapping adapting to varying available capacity; dynamic allocation algorithm adjusting tenant cache usage at runtime.

title: ArbiterQ: Improving QNN Convergency and Accuracy by Applying Personalized Model on Heterogeneous Quantum Devices
problem: In the NISQ era, training and inference on heterogeneous quantum devices is hindered by limited qubits, device noise, and frequent online/offline transitions. Naive distributed QNN approaches destroy accuracy due to device heterogeneity and instability.
method: ArbiterQ applies personalized QNN models for each QPU via two uniform vector representations: model vector (logical-level parameters) and behavioral vector (hardware-level features). By sharing gradients among QPUs with similar behavioral vectors, the framework leverages parallelism while respecting heterogeneity. Additionally, shot-oriented inference scheduling provides fine-grained workload balancing and accuracy optimization.

title: PICACHU: Plug-In CGRA Handling Upcoming Nonlinear Operations in LLMs
problem: Nonlinear operations in LLMs (e.g., softmax, layer norm, GELU, RoPE) contribute significantly to inference latency and are poorly served by fixed-function accelerators designed primarily for matrix multiply/convolution, as they require user-defined precision and flexible dataflow to handle diverse operator shapes and precision requirements.
method: PICACHU uses a Coarse-Grained Reconfigurable Array (CGRA) as a plug-in accelerator specifically targeting nonlinear operations in LLMs. The CGRA is configured with reconfigurable processing elements (PEs) arranged in a spatial dataflow grid that can be reprogrammed per operator, supporting user-defined precision via configurable compute units. PICACHU plugs into existing accelerator pipelines (e.g., alongside a systolic array or GPU) and offloads nonlinear operations while the main compute handles linear algebra. The CGRA dataflow is scheduled at compile time per operator using a mapping tool that assigns CGRA PE configurations and routing to match the operator's precision and shape requirements.

title: Dynamic Local Usage: An Accurate Model for Usage of Tile-Internal Wiring in Global Routing
problem: Traditional global routing treats local wiring usage as a pre-estimated constant, ignoring actual wire-shape geometry and packing density, leading to inaccuracies in routing prediction and detailed routing failures.
method: Dynamic Local Usage (DLU) model evaluates wiring usage based on exact wire shapes and specific pin geometries. Introduces tip-to-tip penalty extensions for accurate packing density modeling. New routing algorithms optimize routes according to DLU congestion. Supports incremental changes like pin movements.

title: Affinity-based Optimizations for TFHE on Processing-in-DRAM
problem: Fully Homomorphic Encryption over the Torus (TFHE) is a compute- and bandwidth-intensive workload; when mapped to Processing-in-Memory (PIM/HBM) architectures, existing accelerators over-exploit parallelism at the expense of data affinity, causing excessive remote data accesses (RDAs) that degrade performance due to PIM's limited inter-bank communication bandwidth.
method: The paper applies algorithmic optimizations to TFHE to restructure its sub-tasks (bootstrapping, key-switching, NTT/FFT operations) so that data accessed together is co-located on the same PIM vault or bank. An offline scheduler analyzes the affinity patterns of TFHE sub-tasks—determining which operands are used together and how frequently—and derives an optimal scheduling order that minimizes RDAs while maintaining sufficient parallelism. The approach is validated on a variant of an existing PIM-HBM device with minimal hardware modifications and evaluated on a real FPGA-based PIM system emulator.

title: Telos: A Dataflow Accelerator for Sparse Triangular Solver of Partial Differential Equations
problem: Sparse triangular solve (SpTRSV) dominates runtime in preconditioned iterative solvers for PDE-derived linear systems due to loop-carried dependencies that severely limit parallelism. Prior accelerators cannot simultaneously achieve high parallelism and good data locality for structured sparsity from stencil-based PDE discretizations.
method: Telos is a dataflow accelerator that exploits structured (stencil-pattern) sparsity in SpTRSV. A plane-parallel pipelining technique maps dependent computations across processing elements (PEs) while preserving data locality within each plane. A cross-plane communication aggregation technique reorganizes inter-plane data transfers into systolic flows, enabling pipelined resolution of loop-carried dependencies with minimal stall overhead. Computation is overlapped with memory accesses to hide latency.

title: EIGEN: Enabling Efficient 3DIC Interconnect with Heterogeneous Dual-Layer Network-on-Active-Interposer
problem: Chiplet-based 3DIC systems using active interposers struggle with heterogeneous and high-load inter-chiplet network traffic patterns because their interconnects are tightly coupled to top-die designs, preventing flexible topology adaptation and causing high latency and traffic congestion.
method: EIGEN implements a heterogeneous dual-layer interconnect on the active interposer: an application-aware switch-programmable layer (AspLayer) for static topology optimization and a dynamic packet-routing layer (DynLayer) for adaptive traffic management. A reinforcement learning (RL)-based path routing framework is trained with a state space covering topology, network, and memory metrics, with reward defined as the product of average packet latency and link utilization. The two layers cooperate to route inter-chiplet traffic with reduced hops and congestion.
